scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8877: Since a firewall change window this morning, BOTH pods
have lost access to every 10.200.0.x server: DNS queries to 10.200.0.2 time
out and no portal loads by name or by IP. Pod-to-pod traffic between
host_1_1_1_1 and host_2_1_1_1 still works. Monitoring shows all OSPF
adjacencies Full and the 10.200.0.0/24 route present on every router.
Identify what is blocking the server farm.

injection.action: add a FORWARD DROP rule for all traffic destined to the server farm

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router_core_3 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: router_core_3 is the mandatory transit for the server farm --
  switch_server_access attaches only to router_core_3 (172.16.0.10/31). The
  new rule `-A FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP` silently discards every
  FORWARDED packet destined to the farm, from both pods. Routing is
  genuinely healthy: OSPF hellos are INPUT/OUTPUT traffic on router_core_3
  (not FORWARD), so all adjacencies stay Full and 10.200.0.0/24 remains in
  every table -- the drop happens at the firewall layer after the routing
  decision. Pod-to-pod traffic transits router_core_1<->router_core_2 and
  matches no rule. Note: router_core_3's OWN pings to the farm still succeed
  (locally generated traffic traverses OUTPUT, not FORWARD) -- a useful
  discriminator.
Localization: router_core_3
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule for destination
  10.200.0.0/24 on router_core_3
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP` on router_core_3
scenario.fix_spec:
remove the DROP rule on router_core_3 --
`iptables -D FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP`

agent.diagnosis_text:
During this morning's firewall change window, a Linux iptables rule was
mistakenly installed in the FORWARD chain of router_core_3. The rule reads:
  -A FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP
It drops every transit packet whose destination falls in the server-farm
prefix 10.200.0.0/24, regardless of source, protocol, or inbound interface.

This explains every observed symptom precisely. router_core_3 is the sole
L3 gateway between the rest of the campus and switch_server_access; all
traffic from either pod must be forwarded through it to reach the server
farm. The FORWARD chain fires on transit packets but NOT on locally
originated ones, which is why router_core_3 itself can ping 10.200.0.2
successfully — those packets traverse the OUTPUT chain and are never
subject to the DROP rule. Pod-to-pod traffic (10.1.1.0/24 ↔ 10.2.1.0/24)
is unaffected because those flows are forwarded through router_core_1 or
router_core_2, neither of which carries any FORWARD rules. The OSPF route
to 10.200.0.0/24 remains present everywhere because iptables operates
entirely independently of the routing plane; the route is installed and
advertised correctly, but packets that match it are silently discarded by
the kernel netfilter hook before they can be sent out. The rule had already
accumulated 10 hits / 840 bytes at the time of inspection.

Root cause: an erroneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule for 10.200.0.0/24 was
added to router_core_3 during the firewall change window.

Corrective fix: on router_core_3, run:
  iptables -D FORWARD 1
This removes rule #1 from the FORWARD chain and immediately restores
forwarding to all servers in the 10.200.0.0/24 farm.
